Immutable

ih-MYOO-tuh-buhl -- from Latin in- ('not') + mutare ('to change'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Immutable is permanent or cannot be changed.

The old monk taught that certain moral truths were immutable, unaffected by fashion or the passing of centuries.

Worked Example

No matter how many times the software is updated, the museum insists that the original architectural plans of the building itself never be altered.

That permanent, unchangeable quality -- something fixed no matter what else changes around it -- is exactly what immutable describes.

How Immutable Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

fixed

fixed: set firmly in place, not changing

unalterable

unalterable: incapable of being changed or altered

Antonyms

mutable

mutable: likely to change

volatile

volatile: liable to change rapidly and unpredictably

How Strong Is It? — fixed → immutable → unalterable

fixed vs. immutable

fixed vs. immutable: Fixed is a milder, more everyday word -- a fixed schedule or fixed price can still technically be changed by someone with authority to do so, while immutable suggests something that cannot be changed under any circumstances.

unalterable vs. immutable

unalterable vs. immutable: Unalterable is nearly identical in strength to immutable, both meaning 'impossible to change,' though immutable is the more formal, often philosophical choice, as in an immutable law of nature.

Put it together

Put it together: Immutable comes from Latin in- ('not') plus mutare ('to change') -- so something immutable is literally 'not changeable,' fixed and permanent no matter what else shifts around it.

Use the root in a new word: mutate

Word Choice

Immutable is a fairly formal, often philosophical or scientific word -- it's commonly paired with 'law,' 'truth,' or 'fact' to describe something treated as permanently fixed, beyond ordinary change.
